A1: No HSSE strategic plan was available for review, and the contractor could not demonstrate a documented program vision, strategic aims or HSSE objectives for the project. Without a strategic plan, HSSE performance cannot be directed or measured against agreed targets. The contractor shall develop the plan and submit it on Aconex for approval.

The HSSE objectives and targets presented during the audit were not included in the approved HSE plan on Aconex. The revised KPIs therefore had no formal status and could not be verified against the Code A submission. The contractor shall revise the HSE plan and resubmit it for approval.

The strategic plan was generic and had not been updated since the previous audit, with no changes reflecting the current project phase, scope or workforce. Objectives that no longer match site conditions do not drive meaningful improvement. The plan shall be reviewed and updated to reflect current risks and activities.

HSSE targets were stated in general terms only, such as zero harm, without measurable leading and lagging KPIs, timeframes or owners. Targets that are not specific and measurable cannot be tracked or used to evaluate performance. The contractor shall define measurable objectives with assigned responsibility.

There was no evidence that HSSE objectives and targets were monitored or reviewed against actual performance during the reporting period. Progress against targets was not presented in management meetings or monthly reports. A periodic review of objective status shall be established and recorded.

Site supervisors and subcontractor representatives interviewed were not aware of the project HSSE vision, strategic aims or annual targets. The strategic plan had not been cascaded beyond senior management, limiting ownership at the workforce level. The contractor shall communicate the objectives through inductions, toolbox talks and notice boards.
A2: The HSSE execution plan was not available on site, and the latest approved revision could not be retrieved from Aconex during the audit. Management could not demonstrate how HSSE roles and responsibilities are delivered on the project. The contractor shall make the Code A plan available and accessible to all key personnel.

The HSSE execution plan reviewed was approved with Code C and had not been revised and resubmitted. Work was proceeding under a plan that had not been accepted by the employer. The contractor shall address all review comments and resubmit the plan on Aconex for approval without delay.

Roles and responsibilities acknowledged by individual positions did not match the Roles and Responsibilities section of the approved HSE plan. Inconsistent definitions create confusion over who is accountable for HSSE duties. The contractor shall align the signed role descriptions with the approved plan.

The HSSE execution plan did not reflect the current organisation chart, as several key management and HSSE positions listed in the plan were vacant or held by different personnel. The plan no longer represented how HSSE is actually managed on site. The organisation chart and plan shall be updated and resubmitted.

Line managers and construction supervisors could not describe their HSSE responsibilities as defined in the execution plan, and no signed acknowledgement records were available. Responsibilities that are not understood are unlikely to be implemented in practice. The contractor shall brief all key personnel and retain signed acknowledgements.

Several commitments in the HSSE execution plan, including inspection frequencies and management site visits, were not being implemented, and no records were available to demonstrate compliance. The plan was treated as a submittal document rather than a working tool. Implementation shall be monitored and the gaps closed.
A3: No training matrix or training needs analysis was available to define the mandatory HSSE, supervisor and construction manager training required for each role. Without it, the contractor cannot confirm that personnel hold the competencies required by NEOM HSAS standards. A role-based training matrix shall be developed and implemented.

The training needs analysis did not include mandatory training for construction leaders and supervisors, such as risk assessment and incident investigation. Key personnel were therefore not identified for required courses. The analysis shall be revised to cover all mandatory courses for every management and supervisory role.

No evidence of qualification was provided for the person delivering the electrical safety course, and no train-the-trainer certificate or equivalent was available. Training delivered by personnel without relevant technical competence may not achieve the required learning outcomes. The contractor shall assign competent trainers for each course.

The training tracker was incomplete and had not been updated, with several employees showing no records of mandatory courses and attendance sheets not matching the tracker entries. Compliance with mandatory training could not be verified. The contractor shall reconcile the records and maintain a current tracker.

Training records showed that refresher training had not been conducted, with some personnel whose last recorded training was the initial site induction more than a year earlier. Expired training was not flagged in the tracking system. The contractor shall schedule refresher courses and implement expiry alerts.

Subcontractor supervisors and HSSE personnel were not included in the contractor training compliance tracking, and no evidence was provided that their mandatory training had been verified. Gaps in subcontractor competence were therefore not visible to management. The contractor shall extend tracking to all subcontractor personnel.
A4: No HSSE audit and inspection schedule was available for the current period, and planned audits and inspections could not be demonstrated. Inspections were being carried out on an ad hoc basis only. The contractor shall develop an annual schedule covering internal audits, subcontractor audits and routine inspections.

An HSSE audit and inspection schedule was in place; however, several planned audits had not been conducted as scheduled and no rescheduling or justification was recorded. Compliance with the schedule was below the planned rate. Overdue audits shall be completed and schedule compliance reported monthly.

In the internal subcontractor monthly audit, an active scope of work was recorded as not applicable, although it formed part of the subcontractor scope. The audit therefore did not assess all ongoing high-risk activities. This was a repeat observation and shall be corrected in the next evaluation.

Scaffolding tag records showed a timeline discrepancy, with a full inspection and tag change from red to green recorded within two minutes. This indicates that inspections may not have been physically performed. The contractor shall verify inspection practices and ensure only a competent person inspects and tags scaffolding.

Findings raised in previous internal audits and inspections were not tracked to closure, and no action log with owners, target dates or close-out evidence was available. Repeat findings were observed during the site tour. A corrective action tracker shall be maintained and reviewed in HSSE meetings.

The audit and inspection schedule did not cover all required equipment and activities, including lifting gear, power tools and electrical distribution boards. These items were therefore not inspected at the frequencies required by NEOM HSAS standards. The schedule shall be expanded and inspection records maintained for each item.
A5: One safety officer recorded zero observation reports for two consecutive months, and the average across the HSE team was below one observation per officer per day. The low reporting rate indicates that the internal observation system was not being used effectively. Individual reporting targets shall be set and monitored.

Monthly HSSE statistics submitted to the employer did not match the contractor internal records, with differences in man-hours, observations and incident counts. Inaccurate data undermines KPI reporting and trend analysis. The contractor shall implement a data verification step before monthly reports are submitted.

HSSE data was collected, but no evidence of trend analysis or evaluation was provided, and the monthly report presented figures without commentary or actions. Data that is not analysed does not support decision making. The contractor shall analyse leading and lagging indicators and identify actions from the trends.

The monthly HSSE report was not submitted within the required timeframe for the last reporting periods, and no record of an agreed extension was available. Delayed reporting prevents the employer from monitoring contractor performance. The contractor shall assign responsibility and ensure reports are submitted on time.

Observation and hazard reports were recorded on paper only and had not been entered into Enablon, resulting in incomplete data on the employer reporting platform. HSSE performance visible to the client was therefore understated. All reportable data shall be uploaded to Enablon within the required timeframe.

There was no documented procedure defining how HSSE data is collected, validated, reported and reviewed by management. Responsibilities for data entry and review were unclear among the HSE team. The contractor shall define the data management process and include it in the HSSE execution plan.
A6: Only a limited number of HSE personnel had active Enablon user accounts, and several supervisors and HSE officers responsible for reporting had no access. Events were therefore relayed verbally and entered later by others. The contractor shall request user access for all personnel with reporting responsibilities.

There was no documented review and validation process for entries made in Enablon, and records were found with missing descriptions, incorrect categories or no supporting photographs. Poor quality data reduces the value of the reporting system. A validation step by a nominated reviewer shall be implemented.

Actions raised in Enablon were not being closed out within their target dates, and a significant number of overdue actions remained open without updates. Overdue actions indicate that identified hazards may remain uncontrolled. The contractor shall review open actions weekly and close them with evidence.

Enablon users had not received training on the system, and HSE officers interviewed could not demonstrate how to raise an observation, record an incident or update an action. Incorrect use of the system leads to incomplete reporting. The contractor shall arrange Enablon training for all registered users.

Incidents and near misses recorded in the contractor internal log were not entered into Enablon within the required timeframe. The employer was therefore not notified through the official reporting system. All incidents shall be reported in Enablon in line with the NEOM incident notification requirements.

No Enablon focal point had been appointed to manage user accounts, monitor data quality and coordinate with the employer HSSE team. Management of the system was informal and dependent on one individual. The contractor shall appoint a focal point and a backup and define their responsibilities.
A7: Incident investigation reports were not available for several recorded incidents, and the investigations that were provided did not include a root cause analysis. Without identifying root causes, effective corrective actions cannot be established. The contractor shall investigate all incidents using a structured root cause methodology.

The level of investigation did not reflect the actual or potential severity of the incident, as a high-potential near miss was investigated only by the site HSE officer. Senior management and competent persons were not involved. Investigation teams shall be assigned according to the severity classification in the NEOM standards.

No evidence was provided that an Incident Review Panel was held for incidents requiring one, and no attendance records or minutes were available. Management review of significant incidents was therefore not demonstrated. The contractor shall convene Incident Review Panels as required and retain the records.

Corrective actions arising from incident investigations were not tracked to closure, and several actions remained open beyond their target dates without follow-up. Similar incidents may recur where actions are not implemented. An action tracker shall be maintained and verified by the HSSE manager.

Lessons learned from recent incidents were not shared with the workforce, and workers interviewed were unaware of the incidents or the preventive measures identified. No toolbox talk records referencing the lessons learned were available. The contractor shall communicate lessons learned and retain attendance records.

Investigation reports were not submitted to the employer within the required timeframe, and the preliminary and final reports were missing from Enablon. This delayed employer review of the incidents. The contractor shall submit investigation reports within the timeframes specified in the NEOM incident reporting requirements.
A8: Safety alerts issued by the employer had not been communicated to the workforce, and no record of distribution or briefing was available for the alerts reviewed. Critical hazard information did not reach those exposed to the risk. The contractor shall brief every alert through toolbox talks and retain records.

HSSE campaigns required by the employer were not implemented, and no evidence of planned campaign activities, materials or attendance records was available. The contractor did not participate in project-wide awareness initiatives. A campaign calendar shall be developed and implemented in line with the employer schedule.

Actions required by safety alerts and lessons learned, such as equipment checks or procedure changes, were not tracked, and there was no evidence that they had been implemented on site. Communication alone does not control the hazard. The contractor shall log required actions and verify their closure.

Communication materials were provided in English only, while a large part of the workforce speaks Arabic, Hindi and Urdu. Workers interviewed could not explain the content of recent alerts. The contractor shall translate key HSSE information into the languages spoken by the workforce.

Notice boards at the site and welfare areas displayed outdated alerts and an old emergency contact number, and the current NEOC emergency numbers were not posted. Outdated information may cause confusion during an emergency. Notice boards shall be reviewed regularly and superseded material removed.

Safety alerts and lessons learned were not cascaded to subcontractors, and subcontractor supervisors confirmed they had not received them. Subcontractor workers therefore remained unaware of recent hazards. The contractor shall include subcontractors in the communication process and obtain acknowledgement of receipt.
A9: No schedule of HSSE meetings was available covering PD and PM HSSE meetings, safety forums and progress and safety meetings. Meetings were held irregularly and without a defined frequency or attendee list. The contractor shall establish a meeting calendar in line with the approved HSE plan.

Attendance records for HSSE meetings showed that the project manager and construction managers did not attend most sessions, and delegates attended in their place. Senior management involvement in HSSE was not demonstrated. The contractor shall ensure mandatory attendance by key management personnel.

Minutes of meetings were not available for several of the HSSE meetings recorded as held, and those available did not list actions, owners or target dates. Decisions taken could not be verified. The contractor shall record minutes for every meeting with a clear action list.

Actions raised in progress and safety meetings were carried forward from meeting to meeting without closure, and no action log was maintained to track status. Repeated open actions indicate that issues were not resolved. The contractor shall maintain an action log and review it at each meeting.

Subcontractors were not invited to the safety forums or weekly HSSE meetings, and no separate subcontractor meetings were held. Subcontractor HSSE issues were therefore not discussed with management. The contractor shall include subcontractor representatives in the meeting program and record their attendance.

Meeting agendas did not include review of HSSE performance, incidents, audit findings or upcoming high-risk activities, and discussion focused on progress only. HSSE matters were not given adequate priority. The contractor shall adopt a standard agenda with HSSE performance as a fixed item.
A10: No documented escalation process was available defining how HSSE non-conformities and overdue corrective actions are escalated to senior management. Escalation depended on individual judgement. The contractor shall define escalation levels, timeframes and responsible persons in the HSSE execution plan.

An escalation process was described in the HSE plan; however, overdue non-conformities had not been escalated as required, and several remained open beyond the defined timeframe. The process was not implemented in practice. Overdue items shall be escalated and their status reported to the project manager.

Non-conformity reports issued by the employer were not logged in a register, and their status, responsible person and closure evidence could not be demonstrated. The contractor could not confirm which items remained open. A non-conformity register shall be maintained and reviewed weekly.

Corrective actions for non-conformities were closed without evidence of implementation, and site verification found the same conditions still present. Closing actions without verification gives a false picture of compliance. The contractor shall require objective evidence and site verification before closure.

Supervisors and HSE officers interviewed were unaware of the escalation process and could not state who should be informed when a corrective action is not completed. Responsibilities for escalation had not been communicated. The contractor shall brief all supervisory and HSE personnel on the process.

Repeat non-conformities from previous audits were identified, and there was no evidence that the recurrence had been escalated or that root causes had been analysed. Repeat findings indicate that corrective actions were ineffective. The contractor shall analyse recurring non-conformities and escalate them to senior management.
A11: No reward and recognition program was in place, and no evidence of recognition awards to workers or supervisors for positive HSSE behaviour was available. Positive reinforcement of safe behaviour was not demonstrated. The contractor shall establish a program with defined criteria and frequency.

A reward and recognition program was described in the HSE plan; however, no awards had been made during the last period and no records of nominations or selections were available. The program was not implemented in practice. The contractor shall implement the program as described in the approved plan.

The reward and recognition program had no defined selection criteria, and awards were given at the discretion of individuals without documented justification. This may be perceived as unfair and reduces the motivational value. Clear and objective criteria shall be defined and communicated to the workforce.

No consequence management process was in place, and no disciplinary action was recorded for serious HSSE violations observed and reported on site. Without consequences, repeated unsafe behaviour is likely to continue. The contractor shall develop a consequence management procedure aligned with the employer requirements.

Consequence management was applied only to workers, and no action was recorded against supervisors or HSE personnel responsible for the activities where violations occurred. Accountability across all levels was not demonstrated. The procedure shall be applied consistently to workers, supervisors and management.

Records of warnings and disciplinary actions were not maintained in a register, and no analysis of violations was carried out to identify repeat offenders or trends. The effectiveness of the consequence process could not be evaluated. The contractor shall maintain a register and review it monthly.
A12: No evidence of monthly HSSE Executive Leadership Meetings was provided, and no schedule for these meetings was available. Senior leadership involvement in HSSE governance was not demonstrated. The contractor shall establish and schedule the meetings with executive attendance as required by the employer.

Executive Leadership Meetings were scheduled monthly; however, records showed that several meetings had been cancelled or postponed without being rescheduled. The required monthly frequency was not maintained. The contractor shall hold the meetings as scheduled and record any changes with justification.

Minutes of meeting for the Executive Leadership Meetings were not available for all sessions held, and those provided were not signed or distributed to attendees. The decisions and commitments made could not be verified. The contractor shall issue approved minutes after every meeting.

No action log was maintained for the Executive Leadership Meetings, and actions recorded in the minutes had no owners or target dates. Follow-up of leadership commitments could not be demonstrated. The contractor shall maintain an action log and review open actions at the start of each meeting.

Attendance records showed that the most senior contractor executives did not attend, and the meetings were chaired by the HSE manager. This did not meet the intent of an executive-level leadership meeting. The contractor shall ensure the project director or equivalent chairs the meeting.

The Executive Leadership Meeting agenda did not cover HSSE performance against KPIs, significant incidents, audit findings or resource needs. Discussions recorded in the minutes were limited to general updates. The contractor shall adopt a structured agenda covering performance and strategic HSSE issues.
A13: No documented work order start up process was available to confirm that HSSE requirements, including approved RAMS, competent personnel and equipment, are in place before work begins. Work packages commenced without a formal readiness review. The contractor shall implement a readiness review with sign-off before start.

Subcontractors were mobilised to site before subcontractor consent was obtained from the employer, and no consent approval records were available for review. Unapproved subcontractors may not meet project HSSE requirements. The contractor shall obtain consent for every subcontractor before mobilisation.

The Subcontractor Management Plan did not include the pre-qualification process, pre-mobilisation process or evaluation scheme. The plan had not been updated since its initial submission. The contractor shall revise the plan to cover these stages and resubmit it on Aconex for approval.

Readiness review records were available; however, checklists were incomplete, with items such as training verification, emergency arrangements and equipment certification left blank. Work was released despite open items. The contractor shall ensure all checklist items are verified before work is authorised to start.

No close out process was in place for completed work orders or demobilising subcontractors, and no records of final HSSE performance evaluation or site handover inspection were available. Lessons from completed scopes were not captured. A close out procedure with HSSE sign-off shall be implemented.

Subcontractor HSSE documentation, including approved RAMS, insurance, personnel competency records and equipment certificates, was not verified before mobilisation, and gaps were found during the audit. The pre-mobilisation review was not effective. The contractor shall verify all documents before subcontractors are allowed on site.
A14: No program for the quarterly Contractor Performance Review was available, and no review had been conducted in the last quarter. HSSE performance was not formally evaluated at management level. The contractor shall establish a quarterly review schedule and include HSSE as a mandatory element.

The quarterly performance review was conducted; however, HSSE performance was not included, and the review covered only progress, cost and quality. The contractor HSSE performance was therefore not evaluated against the agreed KPIs. HSSE shall be included as a weighted section of every review.

The quarterly performance review did not use defined HSSE criteria or scoring, and the HSSE rating was based on general comments without supporting data. The evaluation was subjective and could not be verified. The contractor shall use measurable criteria based on leading and lagging KPIs.

Actions and improvement plans arising from the quarterly performance review were not documented or tracked, and the same weaknesses were repeated in consecutive reviews. The review did not lead to improvement. An improvement plan with owners and target dates shall be developed and followed up.

The contractor did not carry out quarterly performance reviews of its subcontractors, including their HSSE performance, and no evaluation records were available. Poor subcontractor performance could not be identified or addressed. The contractor shall include all subcontractors in the quarterly review process.

Results of the quarterly performance review were not communicated to the project team or subcontractors, and personnel interviewed were unaware of the outcomes. The opportunity to address performance gaps was lost. The contractor shall share review results and the agreed actions with the relevant teams.
A15: No schedule for leadership engagement tours was available, and senior managers carried out site visits on an informal basis only. Leadership visibility on site could not be demonstrated. The contractor shall develop a tour schedule assigning each senior manager a minimum monthly frequency.

Leadership engagement tours were scheduled; however, records showed that the planned frequency was not achieved, and several managers had not completed any tour in the last month. Compliance with the schedule was not monitored. The contractor shall track completion against the schedule and report it monthly.

Leadership tours were recorded only as attendance entries, without details of the areas visited, conversations held, observations made or actions raised. The quality and value of the tours could not be evaluated. The contractor shall use a standard tour form capturing findings and actions.

Actions raised during leadership engagement tours were not tracked to closure, and no tracker linking tour findings to responsible persons and target dates was available. Issues identified by leadership were not followed up. The contractor shall log tour actions and verify their closure.

Leadership tours were limited to office areas and easily accessible locations, and no tours were recorded at high-risk work areas or during night shift activities. Leadership did not engage with workers performing critical tasks. Future tours shall cover high-risk activities and all shifts.

Leadership engagement tours were not measured as an HSSE KPI, and the number and quality of tours were not reported in the monthly HSSE report. Management could not evaluate leadership participation. The contractor shall include tour compliance in KPI reporting and management review.
